summary: Specifies how Ethernet frames are wrapped and carried across an MPLS network inside a pseudowire. This lets providers offer an emulated point-to-point Ethernet service over networks they already run. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4448 specifies how to carry Ethernet frames through an MPLS network using a pseudowire. The pseudowire removes and restores link-specific framing so two endpoints receive an emulated point-to-point Ethernet service.

subtitle: An Ethernet pseudowire carries frames between two sites across an MPLS network.

tldr.problem: A provider may need to connect two Ethernet attachment circuits across a packet-switched network.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress edge strips Ethernet preamble and FCS, adds pseudowire and tunnel encapsulation, and the egress restores the frame for its attachment circuit.
tldr.outcome: The pseudowire emulates a point-to-point Ethernet service between two endpoints. RFC 4448 has been updated by RFC 5462 and RFC 8469.

facts.label: Likely MPLS MTU headroom
facts.value: 8 or more bytes beyond the largest frame

sections.title: An Ethernet Link Through MPLS
sections.content:
An Ethernet pseudowire carries Ethernet protocol data units over a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) network. It assumes a control protocol has already set up the pseudowire and follows the PWE3 architecture.

The service emulates an Ethernet connection between exactly two customer edge endpoints. Although the service resembles a bridged LAN, procedures for more than two customer endpoints are outside this RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire carries Ethernet frames between two endpoints through an MPLS network. The endpoints receive a point-to-point Ethernet service across that network.

sections.title: Provider Edge Processing
sections.content:
Customer equipment connects to provider edge routers over attachment circuits that provide native Ethernet service. The ingress provider edge router encapsulates the frame; the egress router removes the encapsulation and sends the frame through its attachment circuit.

Native Service Processing can strip, overwrite or add VLAN tags, as well as perform other Ethernet-specific processing. The pseudowire termination presents a logical Ethernet port at each end and carries the frame between those points.
sections.plainLanguage: The ingress edge router wraps each frame for transport, and the egress edge router removes the wrapper. Local processing at either edge can handle VLAN tags before or after the pseudowire.

sections.title: Raw Mode and Tagged Mode
sections.content:
Tagged mode uses a service-delimiting 802.1Q VLAN tag on every frame; both ends must understand the tag's meaning. If no service-delimiting tag is present at ingress, the provider edge adds a dummy tag before sending the frame.

Raw mode carries frames from an attachment circuit on one pseudowire and does not send service-delimiting tags across it. The ingress strips that tag when present. In both modes, tags that are not service-delimiting remain part of the carried frame. Tagged mode is the default and the only mode required by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Tagged mode carries a provider tag on each frame so the edges can identify the service. Raw mode removes that provider tag before sending the frame through the pseudowire.

sections.title: Frame Encapsulation and Link Rules
sections.content:
At ingress, the provider edge removes the preamble and Frame Check Sequence (FCS), adds a control word if used, prepends the pseudowire label and tunnel encapsulation, then sends the packet. At egress, it removes the tunnel and pseudowire labels and any control word; Native Service Processing regenerates the FCS.

The pseudowire must not be enabled unless the customer-to-provider MTUs are known to match. Frames larger than the destination interface MTU must be dropped, and frames with hardware CRC or framing errors or a runt condition must be discarded on input. IEEE 802.3x PAUSE frames must not cross the pseudowire.
sections.plainLanguage: The edge removes link-only fields and adds labels for transport. The receiving edge removes those labels and restores the frame for the destination link.

sections.title: The Optional Control Word
sections.content:
The 32-bit control word can sequence frames, help avoid equal-cost multipath misclassification and support operations and management. Its first four bits must be zero; the remaining reserved bits in the first 16 bits are also sent as zero and ignored when received.

The final 16 bits hold a sequence number. Sequence processing is optional, and a value of zero means no sequence check. Because earlier deployments may omit the control word, implementations must be able to send and receive frames without it; the egress must know whether the ingress sends one.
sections.plainLanguage: The optional control word carries a sequence number that can help detect or correct frame reordering. Both edges need to agree on whether it is present.

sections.title: Quality of Service and MTU
sections.content:
A provider edge may use the VLAN user-priority field when choosing quality-of-service treatment in the MPLS network. The edge at the other side may use the encapsulation's quality-of-service field when queuing frames toward the customer. The provider edge must support best-effort carriage.

The MPLS network MTU must fit a maximum-sized Ethernet frame plus the control word, pseudowire label and tunnel encapsulation. With MPLS, the RFC says this is likely to require 8 or more bytes beyond the largest frame. Oversized encapsulated frames must be dropped unless fragmentation and reassembly are used.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider can map frame priority to network service, but must support best-effort transport. The transport network also needs enough MTU for the frame and its encapsulation.

sections.title: Security and Later Updates
sections.content:
The pseudowire's security depends on the security of the MPLS packet-switched network and the general pseudowire control protocol. MAC-address access control and security for virtual bridging are outside the scope of this document.

RFC 4448 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5462 and RFC 8469. Those documents update details of the procedures described here.
sections.plainLanguage: The pseudowire does not provide security beyond that of the underlying MPLS network and its control protocol. Later RFCs update this specification.
